subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 4 of Year 1 Computing at Ehel Academy. The unit is called “Be a Designer”, but do not be fooled by the name — this is not a painting or drawing unit. It is a gentle first taste of coding. The big idea underneath the fun title is one simple sentence: when we change the steps, we change what happens.

There are three small ideas in this unit, and you build on each other. Second, and most important, changing the steps changes the outcome: the word outcome simply means “what happens” or “the result”. A character can move in three ways we can change — how fast it goes (its speed), how far it goes (the number of steps), and which way it goes (the direction). Third, we can guess (predict) what a program will do just by looking at its blocks, and then run it to check if we were right.

outcomes: These come straight from the textbook unit. By the end of the unit, the child should be able to:
Know that an algorithm is a set of instructions (steps) in the right order.
Change an algorithm and understand that this changes the outcome (what happens) — a character can go faster or slower, further or less far, or a different way.
Create an algorithm as a program in ScratchJr by turning each step into a block of code, and run it.
Predict (guess) what happens when a program runs, by looking at its blocks, and then check.

concepts.title: Steps in order (what is an algorithm?)
concepts.explanation:
An algorithm is a set of steps for doing a job, and the steps must be in the right order. We follow algorithms every day without knowing the word.

When we wash our hands, we do the steps in order — we do not dry our hands before we wash them! Steps in the right order are called an algorithm. It is a big word for a simple thing.
concepts.example: Make it a happy chant. Start with something warm and familiar.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you count the hops carefully? Can you follow simple steps one at a time, in order? Do not worry about any coding words yet.

concepts.title: Change the steps, change what happens
concepts.explanation:
This is the heart of the unit. If we change a step, we change the outcome — the outcome just means “what happens”. A moving character can be changed in three ways: how fast (speed), how far (the number of steps), and which way (the direction).

Everyone stands on a start line. Do it with your bodies on the floor. Give a step, then change it, and you can feel the difference.
concepts.example: Find one real example of change the steps, change what happens around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tell that a bigger number of steps goes further? Can you see that these are two different things? Can you tell fast from slow?

concepts.title: Turning steps into blocks (meet ScratchJr)
concepts.explanation:
An algorithm can become a program — steps a tablet can follow. In ScratchJr we do not write words; we join coloured picture blocks. Each block is one step. We can read the blocks to know what the character will do.

First, unplugged, lay out your big paper blocks in a row and “read” them like a story. Teach the colours as a little song, because a child can find a block by its colour long before they can read it
concepts.example: Find one real example of turning steps into blocks (meet ScratchJr) around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you join two or three blocks in a row and tap the green flag to run it? Can you find a block by its colour?

concepts.title: Change a block, change the outcome; and guess first
concepts.explanation:
Now we put Session 2 and Session 3 together. When we change a block in our program, the outcome changes — just like changing a step on the floor. And before we run it, we can predict: look at the blocks and guess what will happen.

Go back to the Rabbit program from last time. Let us make the Rabbit FAST.
concepts.example: Find one real example of change a block, change the outcome; and guess first around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you change the orange speed block and the blue number? Can you see that fast changed the speed, not the finishing place? Do you make a guess BEFORE running?

concepts.title: Be a Program Designer (the Boat project)
concepts.explanation:
You build it, change it to see the outcome change, and predict along the way. This session flows straight into the Mini-Project.

Today you are a Program Designer! We will make a Boat sail across the sea. Then build the algorithm as a program together
concepts.example: Do it yourself: be a Program Designer (the Boat project). Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you choose a change and say what it will do? Can you run it and check? Can you build a working three- or four-block program mostly by themselves?

debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: This is the big one. A child thinks a fast character must also go a long way. Fast means quick; far means a long way. Show two characters that both move 4 steps, one fast and one slow — they stop in the SAME place.

debugging.symptom: A bigger speed number sends it further.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Speed is not a number of steps. The orange Set Speed block only chooses slow, medium, or fast. The blue Move block's number is what changes how far.

debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: The steps must be in the right order, and the yellow start block goes first. Point it out: shoes before socks looks silly.

debugging.symptom: The character can think for itself.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: It cannot. It only does exactly what the blocks say, in order. If it does something odd, we changed a block — it is never the character guessing.

debugging.symptom: Blocks work even with a gap between them.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Blocks must click together in a row like a jigsaw, or only the first one runs. Muddling the arrows. Up, down, left, and right are new. If a character goes the wrong way, check the arrow on the blue block together and point in that direction with your hand. Show a gap failing, then join them.

selfAssessment: I can these come straight from the textbook unit. By the end of the unit, the child should be able to:
I can know that an algorithm is a set of instructions (steps) in the right order.
I can change an algorithm and understand that this changes the outcome (what happens) — a character can go faster or slower, further or less far, or a different way.
I can create an algorithm as a program in ScratchJr by turning each step into a block of code, and run it.
I can predict (guess) what happens when a program runs, by looking at its blocks, and then check.
